Non-metals tend to gain electrons and form negative ions.

items.followUp: Why is the third ionization energy of magnesium greater than its second ionization energy?

rubric.why: After the first ionization, the second electron is removed from the positively charged Mg⁺ ion.
rubric.description: Identifies that the second electron is removed from a positively charged ion.
rubric.how: Look for Mg⁺ or magnesium ion and an indication that the electron is an outer or 3s electron.

rubric.why: The positive ion attracts its remaining electrons more strongly, so more energy is needed.
rubric.description: Explains why the second electron is harder to remove.
rubric.how: Look for stronger nuclear attraction, increased positive charge, or an equivalent explanation.

modelAnswer: Magnesium has the electronic configuration 2,8,2; its first electron is removed from the outer shell to form Mg⁺.
The second electron is removed from this positively charged ion, where the remaining electrons are attracted more strongly to the nucleus.
Therefore, more energy is required for the second ionization than for the first.

items.followUp: Give four differences between an element and a compound.

rubric.why: A compound has a definite composition, whereas a mixture can have variable composition.
rubric.description: Compares the composition of a compound and a mixture.
rubric.how: Look for fixed or definite composition contrasted with variable composition or ratio.

rubric.why: The components of a compound are chemically combined; those of a mixture are physically mixed.
rubric.description: Compares how the substances are joined.
rubric.how: Look for chemical combination contrasted with physical mixing.

rubric.why: A compound has properties different from its constituent elements, while mixture components retain their properties.
rubric.description: Compares the properties of the components and the resulting material.
rubric.how: Look for new or different compound properties contrasted with retained component properties.

rubric.why: Compounds are separated by chemical methods, while mixtures can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.description: Compares methods of separation.
rubric.how: Look for chemical separation contrasted with physical separation.

rubric.why: A compound has a definite chemical formula; a mixture does not have a fixed formula.
rubric.description: Compares the formula representation of each.
rubric.how: Look for a definite formula for compounds contrasted with no fixed formula for mixtures.

modelAnswer: A compound has a fixed composition; a mixture has a variable composition.
The elements in a compound are chemically combined; the substances in a mixture are physically mixed.
A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements; the components of a mixture retain their properties.
A compound can be separated into its elements by chemical methods; a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
A compound has a definite chemical formula; a mixture has no fixed chemical formula.

items.followUp: Define hydrogen bonding and describe two effects it has on the physical properties of water.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding involves hydrogen covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom such as F, O, or N.
rubric.description: Identifies the required hydrogen-to-electronegative-atom bond.
rubric.how: Look for hydrogen together with fluorine, oxygen, or nitrogen.

rubric.why: The hydrogen is attracted to an electronegative atom or lone pair in a neighbouring molecule.
rubric.description: Defines the attraction between molecules.
rubric.how: Look for an intermolecular attraction involving hydrogen.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding increases the energy needed to separate molecules, raising boiling or melting points.
rubric.description: States an effect on melting or boiling point.
rubric.how: Look for a high or increased melting/boiling point.

rubric.why: Intermolecular attraction can increase viscosity or surface tension.
rubric.description: States an effect on viscosity or surface tension.
rubric.how: Look for viscosity or surface tension being increased or unusually high.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding can reduce volatility and affects solubility in water.
rubric.description: States another physical-property effect of hydrogen bonding.
rubric.how: Look for reduced volatility or an effect on water solubility.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is the intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to F, O, or N and an electronegative atom of a neighbouring molecule.
Hydrogen bonding holds molecules together and raises their boiling and melting points.
It can also increase viscosity and surface tension.
It reduces volatility and influences the solubility of compounds in water.

items.followUp: Define evaporation and describe the effect of temperature, surface area and humidity on its rate.

rubric.why: Evaporation is the escape of surface molecules into vapour, and can occur below the boiling point.
rubric.description: Defines evaporation.
rubric.how: Look for liquid surface molecules changing into vapour.

rubric.why: Higher temperature and a larger exposed surface area increase the rate of evaporation.
rubric.description: Explains the effects of temperature and surface area.
rubric.how: Look for both factors and the correct increase in rate.

rubric.why: Moving air carries vapour away, while high humidity slows evaporation.
rubric.description: Explains the effects of wind and humidity.
rubric.how: Look for wind or air movement increasing the rate and/or humidity decreasing it.

rubric.why: The nature of the liquid affects how readily its molecules escape.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of the liquid's nature.
rubric.how: Look for volatility or intermolecular forces linked to the rate.

modelAnswer: Evaporation is the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface, at a temperature below its boiling point.
Increasing the temperature or the exposed surface area increases the rate of evaporation.
Greater wind speed increases evaporation by carrying vapour away; greater humidity decreases it.
The nature of the liquid also matters: more volatile liquids evaporate faster.

items.followUp: Give four characteristics of a colloidal solution.

rubric.why: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture.
rubric.description: Identifies the heterogeneous nature of a suspension.
rubric.how: Look for the term heterogeneous or an equivalent description.

rubric.why: Suspended particles are relatively large and can be seen.
rubric.description: Describes the particles in a suspension.
rubric.how: Look for particles described as large or visible.

rubric.why: Suspended particles settle on standing.
rubric.description: States that particles settle out over time.
rubric.how: Look for settling or sediment formation when left undisturbed.

rubric.why: Suspension particles can be separated by filtration.
rubric.description: Gives a method of separating the particles.
rubric.how: Look for filtration or a filter.

modelAnswer: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture.
Its particles are large enough to be visible.
The particles settle down when the suspension is left standing.
The particles can be separated from the liquid by filtration.
